title: Load Balancing
summary: Understand what a load balancer does, L4 vs L7, the main balancing algorithms, health checks, sticky sessions and how traffic is spread across regions.

questions.prompt: What problems does a load balancer solve? Name at least three.
questions.hint: Think about scale, failures and deployments.
keyPoints: Spreads requests across many servers so you can scale out
Detects unhealthy servers with health checks and stops sending them traffic (availability)
Gives clients one stable address so servers can be added, removed or upgraded without clients noticing (rolling deploys)
Can also terminate TLS and route by path/host (at L7)

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between an **L4** and an **L7** load balancer. You need to route `/api/*` to one server pool and `/static/*` to another: which do you need, and why?
questions.hint: Which layer can actually read the URL?
keyPoints: L4 works with TCP/UDP connections, IPs and ports; it does not read HTTP content
L7 terminates the connection and parses HTTP, so it can see paths, headers and cookies
Path-based routing needs L7, because the path is inside the HTTP request
L4 is faster and protocol-agnostic; L7 enables TLS termination, retries and smarter routing at more CPU cost

questions.prompt: Your servers are behind a round-robin load balancer. Most requests take 5 ms, but about 1% are report exports that take 20 seconds. Users complain that sometimes even simple pages are slow. What's going on, and what would you change?
questions.hint: Round robin balances the number of requests, not the amount of work.
keyPoints: Round robin ignores how busy each server is, so slow exports pile up on some servers by chance and fast requests queue behind them
Switch to least connections (or least response time / power of two choices) so new requests avoid busy servers
Better still, move slow exports off the request path: put them on a queue processed by background workers (Day 34) and notify when done
Or route exports to a separate pool with an L7 rule so they can't hurt interactive traffic

questions.prompt: A load balancer runs health checks every **10 seconds** with a **2-second timeout** and marks a server unhealthy after **3 consecutive failures**. A server crashes right after passing a check. In the worst case, roughly how long until it's removed? If that server was receiving **500 requests/second**, how many requests might fail in that window, and how could you reduce that?
questions.hint: The first failing check happens up to one interval later. Each check may wait for the timeout.
keyPoints: Three failed checks are needed: at about 10 s, 20 s and 30 s after the crash, the last one taking up to 2 s more to time out
So roughly 30–32 seconds of being in rotation while dead
500 req/s × ~30 s ≈ 15,000–16,000 failed requests (if the LB doesn't retry)
Reduce by checking more often or needing fewer failures (risk: flapping), adding passive health checks/outlier detection, and retrying idempotent requests on another server
questions.answer: Checks at ~10, 20, 30 s after the crash (+ up to 2 s timeout) → removed after **≈ 30–32 s**. `500 × 30 ≈ 15,000` failed requests. Fix with passive checks (eject on real errors), shorter intervals, and LB retries for idempotent requests.

questions.prompt: Implement **weighted round robin** in JavaScript. Given `[{name: 'A', weight: 5}, {name: 'B', weight: 1}, {name: 'C', weight: 1}]`, every 7 calls to `pick()` should return A five times, B once and C once. Bonus: spread them out instead of returning `AAAAABC`.
questions.hint: Simplest version: expand the list by weight. For the bonus, look up "smooth weighted round robin" (used by Nginx): keep a running score per server.
keyPoints: Simple version builds an expanded list (A, A, A, A, A, B, C) and round-robins over it
Each server receives traffic in proportion to its weight
Smooth version: every pick, add each server's weight to its current score, choose the highest score, then subtract the total weight from the chosen one
Smooth version for A:5, B:1, C:1 gives AABACAA, interleaving B and C instead of bunching all the A's together

questions.prompt: You run a chat service with users worldwide and data centers in the US, Europe and Asia. Each data center has many WebSocket servers. Design the load-balancing layers from the user's device down to a single WebSocket server, including what happens when a whole region fails.
questions.hint: Think global (which region?), then regional (which server?), and remember WebSocket connections are long-lived.
keyPoints: Global layer: GeoDNS or anycast sends each user to the nearest healthy region; short DNS TTLs or anycast route withdrawal for failover
Regional layer: redundant L4 load balancers (or L4 in front of an L7 fleet) across availability zones; the LB itself is not a single point of failure
Use least connections (not round robin) because WebSocket connections are long-lived and uneven
Health checks remove dead servers; clients reconnect with backoff and land on a healthy server
On region failure, traffic shifts to other regions, which need spare capacity, and a reconnect storm must be absorbed (jittered reconnects)
